name: Prize crossword No 24,963
preamble: Abbreviations, all of a kind, at the beginning or end of ten solutions have been ignored in the clues

clue.text: Bud's turned to flower but I stick to the root, so to speak

definitions.text: I stick to the root, so to speak

indicators.note: something turned has been twisted out of its first shape, so these letters take a new order

blocks.note: taken as written, apostrophe dropped
a river is a flow-er, something that flows

explanation.surface: A gardener's note: the bud has opened into a flower, but the speaker stays stubbornly down at the root.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flower' looks like a bloom but is the crossword's favourite river, something that flows. In the definition, 'root' said aloud is 'route', which a bus driver must stick to.
explanation.definitionFit: A bus driver keeps to a fixed route, and 'root' and 'route' are pronounced alike in British speech.

clue.text: Flower employs second spinner

blocks.note: B is the second letter and the mark for second class or second grade
a loom is a machine for making cloth from yarn, loosely a spinner

explanation.surface: A flower seems to hire a second spinner, perhaps a spider or a top.
explanation.walkthrough: B stands for second, as in B-grade or the second letter; 'employs' just joins the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A bloom is a blossom, the flowering part of a plant, so the two nouns are direct synonyms.

clue.text: Attendant student among the cream

indicators.note: to be among others is to be surrounded by them, so one piece goes inside

blocks.note: L is a learner, the plate on a learner driver's car
the cream of society is its elite

explanation.surface: A student mingles with the cream of society, perhaps as a hanger-on.
explanation.walkthrough: SAT for Saturday begins the answer but is not clued, as the preamble warns; the rest is a learner set inside the elite.
explanation.definitionFit: A satellite is a hanger-on or follower that waits on someone more important, just as an attendant does.

clue.text: Mask for robber unfinished in similar holiday spot

indicators.note: work left unfinished lacks its end, so the final letter goes
the second word is treated in the same way as the first, so it too loses its ending
one piece sits inside the other, held between its letters

blocks.note: a pirate is a robber at sea
a seaside resort is a holiday spot

explanation.surface: A disguise for a robber who is hiding out in a holiday resort.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Similar' tells you that the holiday spot is also unfinished, so both words lose their last letter before one goes inside the other.
explanation.definitionFit: A respirator is a mask worn over the nose and mouth to filter the air breathed in.

clue.text: Qualities of 6 the last to recover

indicators.note: the last one in a line is the one at its end, so only the final letter is kept

blocks.note: the number six in Roman numerals
the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: Someone lists the strengths of the person in clue 6, last in a race to get well.
explanation.walkthrough: '6' looks like a cross-reference to another clue, but it is simply the number in Roman numerals. TUES for Tuesday ends the answer unclued, as the preamble warns.
explanation.definitionFit: Virtues are good qualities of character, such as honesty or patience, so the plural nouns match.

clue.text: Small piles of hay perhaps cause complaint

blocks.note: a rick is a stack of hay, and '-et' makes a little one, so this is a playful made-up plural
the bone-softening illness of children caused by lack of vitamin D

explanation.surface: Little haystacks are blamed for some ailment on the farm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' admits the first sense is invented: a rick is a haystack and '-et' a diminutive ending, as in 'islet'.
explanation.definitionFit: A complaint is an illness, and rickets is a childhood disease that softens the bones through vitamin D deficiency.

clue.text: Sticker, say, in reverse

indicators.note: going in reverse means travelling backwards, so the letters are read from the end

blocks.note: e.g. means 'for example', as 'say' does

explanation.surface: A label or badge described, oddly, as being in reverse.
explanation.walkthrough: WED for Wednesday starts the answer unclued, as the preamble warns, so only the last two letters come from the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A wedge is jammed into a gap to hold something fast, so it is literally a thing that sticks.

clue.text: Cover with words and music

blocks.note: W is a standard abbreviation for with
rap is spoken words delivered over music

explanation.surface: A cover version of a song, complete with lyrics and tune.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cover' tempts you toward a cover version of a song, but it is the verb meaning to enclose.
explanation.definitionFit: To wrap something is to enclose it in paper or cloth, which is one sense of the verb to cover.

clue.text: Devilishly good player of successive notes

blocks.note: D and E are neighbouring notes of the musical scale

explanation.surface: A musician who plays runs of notes with devilish skill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Player' suggests a musician, but it is the definition's sportsman; MON for Monday ends the answer unclued, as the preamble warns.
explanation.definitionFit: Calling someone a demon at a game is an idiom for a fiercely skilful competitor, as in a demon bowler.

clue.text: Stop press: binding security provided

blocks.note: to stop is to end
the press is the newspapers

explanation.surface: A newspaper's 'stop press' notice about some binding security deal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stop press' looks like one newsroom phrase but splits into two separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Endpapers are the sheets pasted inside a book's covers, securing the pages to the binding.

clue.text: Victim of cold porridge, reportedly

indicators.note: something reported is passed on by word of mouth, so the sound matters, not the spelling

blocks.note: porridge is made from oats

explanation.surface: Someone fell ill after eating cold porridge, so the story goes.
explanation.walkthrough: Captain Lawrence Oates died in the Antarctic on Scott's 1912 expedition, walking out into a blizzard.
explanation.definitionFit: Captain Oates perished of exposure in the polar snow, so he was literally a victim of the cold.

clue.text: Cider drunk with meal — such is Fenland

indicators.note: a drunk person is unsteady and muddled, so these letters lurch into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Cider taken with a meal is said to be typical of the Fens.
explanation.walkthrough: The Fens are low marshland in eastern England, drained from the 1600s onward to make farmland.
explanation.definitionFit: Fenland is land won back from marsh and sea by drainage, which is what reclaimed land means.

clue.text: Crowds with crosses in which 9 nearly died

indicators.note: nearly means not quite all, so the last letter is cut
the words point to something placed inside the earlier piece

blocks.note: a mule is a cross between a horse and a donkey
clue 9's answer leads to Titus Oates, the Popish Plot informer
d. is the abbreviation for died

explanation.surface: Crowds bearing crosses, perhaps at a memorial where someone nearly lost their life.
explanation.walkthrough: Clue 9 is a different Oates here: Titus Oates, the 17th-century perjurer who was flogged almost to death. His first name, minus its last letter, goes inside the hybrids with D.
explanation.definitionFit: Multitudes are great numbers of people gathered together, which is what crowds are.

clue.text: South American in state

blocks.note: taken as written
CA is the postal abbreviation for California

explanation.surface: A South American dignitary lies in state.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In state' reads like a phrase about pomp, but the state is California.
explanation.definitionFit: The Inca were a native people of the Andes in Peru, so an Inca is one kind of South American.

clue.text: His return was foretold when family paper turned up

indicators.note: in a down clue, turning something up flips it to read from the bottom

blocks.note: kin are relatives
a rag is a disparaging word for a newspaper

explanation.surface: A prophecy of someone's homecoming when the family newspaper finally showed up.
explanation.walkthrough: THUR for Thursday ends the answer unclued, as the preamble warns.
explanation.definitionFit: Legend calls Arthur 'the once and future king', sleeping until Britain needs him, so his coming back was prophesied.

clue.text: What tinker says about nationalists' piece of armour

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece wraps round the other

blocks.note: a tinker's cuss is a proverbial worthless oath
the Irish Republican Army, Irish nationalists

explanation.surface: A travelling tinker comments on the nationalists' armour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not worth a tinker's cuss' is a British idiom; a tinker was a travelling mender of pots, and a cuss is a curse.
explanation.definitionFit: A cuirass is a breastplate and backplate fastened together, worn to protect a soldier's torso.

clue.text: Spooner's dominant quality that keeps house together

indicators.note: the Reverend Spooner swapped the opening sounds of words, so the starts trade places

blocks.note: the boss is the dominant one in charge
cream means the top quality, the best
the two pieces spoken together, ready for their opening sounds to trade

explanation.surface: Spooner's commanding personality is what holds his household together.
explanation.walkthrough: Swap the opening sounds of the two pieces and the first loses its B for a CR while the second gains it.
explanation.definitionFit: A crossbeam is a horizontal timber spanning a building, tying the walls and roof structurally into one.

clue.text: Fairy swimmers coming back with a slight cold?

indicators.note: coming back is returning the way one came, so the letters run right to left

blocks.note: an elf is a fairy creature
fins are what a fish swims with

explanation.surface: A fairy returns from swimming having caught a chill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swimmers' looks like people in the water, but it means the fins that do the swimming.
explanation.definitionFit: A sniffle is a minor head cold with a runny nose, the mildest kind of the illness.

clue.text: Dish has direction in case

indicators.note: one piece sits inside the other, held between its letters

blocks.note: south-east, a compass direction
taken as written

explanation.surface: A recipe dish comes with directions in its box.
explanation.walkthrough: FRI for Friday begins the answer unclued, as the preamble warns.
explanation.definitionFit: A fricassee is a stew of sliced meat, usually chicken, in a white sauce, served as a dish.

clue.text: Needing hard work to make America finally love an emperor

indicators.note: finally means at the end, so this piece is placed last

blocks.note: love is zero in tennis, shaped like O
Nero was an emperor of Rome
the United States

explanation.surface: It takes real effort to make America finally fall for an emperor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Finally' looks like it picks a last letter, but it only puts America at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Onerous tasks are burdensome and laborious, demanding heavy effort, which is what needing hard work describes.

clue.text: I leave Arab to eat starter (cooked)

indicators.note: when the letter walks out it is removed from the word
something eaten goes inside the eater, so one piece swallows another

blocks.note: a Saudi is an Arab from Saudi Arabia
the tee is where each golf hole starts

explanation.surface: An Arab diner skips a dish and eats only the starter, which was cooked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Starter' wants to be a first course in this dining scene, but it is the golf tee, where play on a hole starts.
explanation.definitionFit: Sautéed means fried quickly in a little hot fat, one particular way of having cooked food.

clue.text: One taking his turn to make traps for germs?

blocks.note: a bug is a germ or infection
a gin is a snare or trap for game

explanation.surface: Someone takes a turn at building traps to catch germs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Buggins' turn' is a British phrase for handing out jobs by rotation rather than merit. The question mark flags the surface's odd germ traps.
explanation.definitionFit: Buggins is the imaginary person whose turn it is in the idiom 'Buggins' turn', promotion by rota.

clue.text: But stay uncloth'd if this is prescribed

definitions.text: But stay uncloth'd if this is prescribed

blocks.note: surface reading: a poetic plea to stop and remain undressed
setter's reading: a doctor's order to stay put in your nightclothes, lying down

explanation.surface: A line of old verse, with its clipped 'uncloth'd', begging a lover to stay undressed.
explanation.walkthrough: The archaic spelling makes it read like poetry, but the scene is medical: a patient ordered to stay undressed and lying down.
explanation.definitionFit: Doctors prescribe a spell lying down to recover from illness, and patients then stay out of day clothes.

clue.text: Laments for Mass Observation

indicators.note: the word stands in for its answer, which is held inside the words that follow

blocks.note: the letters run across the join of the two words

explanation.surface: Mourning recorded by Mass Observation, the British social-research project that collected ordinary people's diaries.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mass Observation' reads as one name, and the answer runs straight through the middle of it.
explanation.definitionFit: Laments are cries of grief, and sobs are the convulsive weeping sounds that express that grief.

clue.text: Sailor with personal problem

blocks.note: BO is body odour, a classic personal problem

explanation.surface: A seaman with an embarrassing personal issue.
explanation.walkthrough: SUN for Sunday ends the answer unclued, as the preamble warns; 'personal problem' is a coy euphemism for body odour.
explanation.definitionFit: A bosun, or boatswain, is the ship's officer in charge of rigging and deck crew, a seaman.

clue.text: City of the region in Germany

indicators.note: the words tell you to translate into the German language

blocks.note: der is a German form of 'the', used in the genitive to mean 'of the'
a German Land is a region or federal state

explanation.surface: A city of some region in Germany.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue sounds as if the city is German, but 'in Germany' just asks for German words; SUN for Sunday begins the answer unclued.
explanation.definitionFit: Sunderland is a port city in north-east England on the River Wear, granted city status in 1992.

clue.text: Old copper on beat was resident

blocks.note: d was the abbreviation for the old British penny, a copper coin
to welt is to beat or thrash

explanation.surface: An old policeman on his beat lived locally.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Copper' and 'beat' paint a police officer on patrol, but the copper is a coin: d was the old penny before 1971.
explanation.definitionFit: To dwell is to live in a place, so dwelt is the past tense meaning lived there, was resident.

clue.text: Had nothing to pay

blocks.note: O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A debtor confesses they had no money at all to settle the bill.
explanation.walkthrough: With WED for Wednesday ignored, only the first letter is clued, and the whole clue also describes a debtor with nothing to pay.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who owed had a debt outstanding, money still due because they had nothing to pay it with.

clue.text: Half 11, about — join the lady in another column

indicators.note: half a word keeps one part of it and drops the rest
about means around, so the first piece wraps round what follows

blocks.note: the number written as a word
to sew is to join with thread
her refers to a woman

explanation.surface: A newspaper note: half of item 11 is continued in another column, alongside the lady's piece.
explanation.walkthrough: '11' looks like a cross-reference to 11 across, but here it is just the number spelt out.
explanation.definitionFit: Elsewhere means in some other place, and a different column of the paper is another place.

clue.text: Hurry has the heart displaced

indicators.note: the heart is the middle, and displacing it moves it out of the word

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written, before its middle letter goes

explanation.surface: Rushing about leaves one's heart out of place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heart' is the middle letter of the short word, not an organ.
explanation.definitionFit: Haste is speed or urgency in action, and hurry is a direct noun synonym for it.

clue.text: God after Christ?

blocks.note: AD, anno Domini, marks years after Christ's birth

explanation.walkthrough: MON for Monday begins the answer unclued, as the preamble warns; the question mark flags the theological puzzle of a god coming after Christ.
explanation.definitionFit: In philosophy, especially Leibniz and the Neoplatonists, the Monad is the supreme indivisible One, a name for God.

clue.text: Put fellow off using cleaner

blocks.note: read together with 'off' at the end, to put off is to deter
a gent is a gentleman, a fellow

explanation.surface: Someone was put off by a man using cleaning products.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put ... off' is a split phrase with the fellow sitting in the middle; the order of pieces follows the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Detergent is a chemical cleaning agent, such as washing powder, so it is a kind of cleaner.
